idiom_name: module privacy plus restricted visibility (pub(in path), pub(super), pub(crate)); the granting module subtree is the attorney
implementation_notes: Rust has the grant as syntax rather than as a structure: everything is private by default, a private item is reachable from its module and its descendants, and visibility can be restricted to a named ancestor module with pub(in path) - equivalently pub(super), pub(crate), pub(self) - while pub(in path) may only name an ancestor, so where the item is declared is what expresses the grant (Rust Reference, visibility and privacy). The idiomatic realization is therefore structural: declare the implementation in a module that is an ancestor of the helper, mark only the granted operations pub(in that module) (or pub(super)), and the compiler rejects every path from outside the subtree. A hand-built forwarding type is still justified when the granted surface must be narrower than the items themselves - exposing one operation while the underlying fields stay private - or when two consumers must receive different slices.
pitfalls: pub(in path) accepts only an ancestor module: a grant to a sibling is impossible, so the collaborator must be moved under the granting module (or the grant widened to pub(crate)) - that structural decision is the pattern in Rust.
pub(crate) is the tempting over-grant: it hands the implementation to every module in the crate, present and future, which is exactly what the narrow grant was meant to avoid.

Visibility is per item and constrains signatures: a restricted function whose parameter or return type is even more private trips the private-interface check (E0446), so the granted surface and the types it names must be restricted compatibly.
